rv.q: The laughs Lois got in that moment were bigger and truer than anything else in the production, all because the sheep wasn’t trying and was just, accidentally, in the moment.
The Tates’ fridge is almost always empty, and there’s a similar sense of vacancy to the direction and performances in the New Group’s lackluster production of this 1977. Sam Shepard play.

The intensity of Shepard’s writing—which segues dazzlingly from brutal to whimsical to extravagantly operatic—is matched in director Scott Elliott’s impressive staging in one of Signature’s smallest spaces.
The poison has been absorbed, and luckily for us, if not for them, it’s lost none of its potency.
Curse of the Starving Class remains an enticing family drama that will keep you up at night wondering if we can escape our own fates.
Nonetheless, director Terry Kinney’s solid revival for the Signature Theatre Company remains compelling throughout its entire 2 ½-hour running time, thanks largely to Shepard’s pungent dialogue.
But I’ve begun to think that this play might require meatier direction to keep the audience from leaving hungry.
This revival of Curse of the Starving Class isn’t cursed but it also doesn’t cast any spells.
What’s ironic is that the real warning should have been to advise audience members that they’ll be bored to tears during the course of this miscast, indifferently staged, sluggish revival.
Unexciting, emotionally uninvolving…Few moments find the right balance between Shepard's earthy realism and his poetic demands.
To breathe theatrical life into this wild clan—and Shepard’s scorching dialogue—demands a degree of intensity that Scott Elliot’s production just can’t provide.
This is a “Curse of the Starving Class” that will be difficult to match in its perfection and its stark examination of a family system gone wrong of its own accord.
Nevertheless, the cast is excellent, fearlessly handling the text’s demanding ricocheting between absurdity and intense – often ferociously violent – realism.

The design elements have all been building toward the seismic explosion – the lighting letting everyone speak freely to the audience for a moment stoked the metaphorical fires, the sound fanned the dramatic tension to the flames.

While The New Group’s production of Curse of the Starving Class has its moments of the darkest kind of humor, it is in essence a tragic look at a desperate nuclear family that is failed by society and, above all, has failed themselves and each other, as with the innocent sheep.
The part that matters here is that we (meaning me) ended up not caring about any of these people.
The New Group’s Curse falters in spirit, flaying around a bit too much in the anger and madness, while never really finding the poetry of the moment.
There's an even-keeled sameyness to the cast's portrayals that undercuts the reversals that Shepard unleashes in the final act.

cn.t: This revival of Shepard's family dysfunction drama earns mixed reviews, with critics divided on Scott Elliott's direction. While some praise the intensity and performances (especially the live sheep), many find it emotionally flat and lackluster.
